source.version_note: Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications 11, article 36, published 30 April 2026. Received 13 March 2025 and accepted 23 March 2026; a later third experiment is not by itself a contradictory publication date.
source.verification_method: All 24 supplied text pages, ten figures, six tables, declarations and bibliography read. Figures inspected as rendered pages, including the unequal warning icons. Publisher and Crossref verify main identity/date. All fields of three public AsPredicted records read; OSF file inventory inspected. Targeted bibliography checks distinguish a journal article from its later chapter version. No original model output or participant-level reanalysis.

citation.title: Warning people about the risk of AI error mitigates human acquisition of AI bias

reading.source_scope_note: Three fictional tissue-classification experiments study following scripted erroneous advice and immediate same-task errors after advice withdrawal. These are 616 retained participations, not clinicians, real patients, a deployed AI or delayed clinical discrimination. The warning headline is qualified by its direct comparisons and null outcomes.
access_limits: All ten figures and six tables read. Figure 1 changes both accuracy wording and the warning icon; Figure 6 similarly adds an icon to the general-warning condition. Thus the manipulations are communication packages, not isolated wording-only effects.

All eight substantive fields of three public AsPredicted records read through their public HTML renderings. Direct PDF downloads returned 403. Registration statements and visible dates were inspected, not independently authenticated against collection logs.

The public OSF h2gmz inventory lists three CSV datasets and three data notebooks. Selected notebook download attempts are recorded separately. Inventory inspection alone is not reading or reproducing the files. No participant dataset or statistical code was executed.

Cited books, previous experiments and original framing studies were not independently fully read here. Targeted bibliographic metadata and chapter-identity checks receive no additional full-reading credit. No private archive, author contact or participant records sought.

study.sample: Experiment 1: 179 recruited, four excluded, 175 retained across negative framing n64, positive framing n52 and no-information n59. Experiment 2: 200 recruited, two technical exclusions, 198 retained, warning n100 and no-information n98. Experiment 3: 254 recruited, nine practice failures and two chance-performance exclusions, 243 retained across warned AI n81, unwarned AI n84 and warned unassisted n78. These sum to 616 retained participations, not independently verified unique people.
study.fictional_task: Participants imagine clinicians and classify simulated pink/light tissue images for a fictitious syndrome using instructed majority-color rules. The disease, tissues, patients and advisor are fictitious; no diagnostic expertise or clinical harm outcome is observed. Instructions counterbalance which majority color means positive versus negative.
study.practice_selection: Twelve practice trials comprise six corrective-feedback trials and six randomized trials. Participants must achieve at least five of six correct in the latter, with another instruction/practice opportunity. Phase 1 accuracy also determines inclusion, making it a post-assignment selection criterion. Registration specifies more than 30 correct of 60; the article wording varies at the exact 30 threshold.
study.advice: The scripted AI is wrong on all ten trials of one selected image class out of 60 assisted trials: 16.7% wrong and 83.3% correct. Experiment 1 labels this 20% wrong/80% correct and explicitly discloses rounding for simpler instructions. Do not describe that mismatch as undisclosed. It does not establish how actual model error uncertainty should be communicated.
study.sequence: The biased class is excluded from the first ten assisted trials to avoid an initial negative impression; trial order is otherwise randomized subject to constraints. Phase 2 is 25 unassisted trials, including five ambiguous 50/50 images and five each of four nonambiguous classes. Three analysis blocks each contain five biased-class trials: two assisted bins and one unassisted bin. They are analysis groupings, not separate interventions.
study.error_types: Experiment 1 places all errors on 40/60 images. Experiments 2–3 switch to 60/40 images. Counterbalanced positive/negative labels determine whether the scripted error is a false positive or false negative. Participants are nonexperts; error costs are not separately manipulated or measured. Perceptual color direction and diagnosis label are related design factors, not actual clinical consequences.
study.experiment_1_tests: The 3-group × 3-block model has a real interaction, F(4,344) 4.05, p .003, group F(2,172) 3.82, p .024 and block F(2,344) 14.27, p < .001. The reported corrected group difference is negative framing versus no information only in Block 2, t(172) 3.41, p .022. Negative versus positive framing in that block is nonsignificant, p .997; positive versus no information p .262. No group difference is reported in Block 1 or the unassisted Block 3.
study.experiment_1_transfer: Ambiguous-image generalization has no group effect, F(2,172) .935, p .395. The two-factor instruction/group analysis reports group p .068 in Phase 1 and .129 in Phase 2, with several group/interaction numerator degrees of freedom mislabeled as one. An exploratory instruction effect does not establish a warning benefit in the unassisted phase.
study.experiment_2_tests: The 2-group × 2-error-type × 3-block model reports a warning-group main effect, F(1,194) 7.95, p .005. Error-type main effect p .269, group × error p .111, group × block p .627 and three-way p .716 are nonsignificant. Preserve the real overall warning association; do not invent a false-positive-specific moderation from unequal exploratory pairwise significance.
study.experiment_2_generalization: Ambiguous-image means .59 warned versus .66 unwarned yield t(196) −1.09, p .276. No supported warning effect on that generalization outcome. Reported error detection is higher, 93% versus 81.6%, chi-squared 5.80, p .016. Follow-up perceived-error comparisons are restricted to participants reporting detected errors; these are not all 198 participants.
study.experiment_3_design: Adds a group warned about AI error that never receives AI. Both assisted groups lose assistance in Phase 2, and explicit on/off indicators make availability salient. There is no unwarned unassisted arm, so this is not a full warning × AI factorial design.
study.experiment_3_tests: The preregistered 3-group × 2-error-type × 3-block ANOVA reports group F(2,237) 20.076, p < .001 and group × block F(4,474) 7.111, p < .001. Type of error p .060, group × error p .618 and three-way p .851 do not support the proposed type-specific warning effect. The authors explicitly acknowledge this null moderation.
study.experiment_3_direct_comparison: In the unassisted Block 3, warned-AI versus unwarned-AI is reported nonsignificant. Warned-AI versus always-unassisted p .485 is also nonsignificant, whereas unwarned-AI versus always-unassisted p .001 is significant. These two comparisons against control do not establish a direct warning benefit or equivalence of warned and unassisted groups. Table 6 means are .15, .24 and .06, respectively; these are descriptive means, not a new significance test.
study.experiment_3_generalization: The three-group ambiguous-image ANOVA has F(2,237) 11.87, p < .001, with no error-type main effect or interaction. Figure 10 shows both previously assisted groups more directionally aligned than the unassisted group. No pairwise warning contrast is supplied here; ambiguous 50/50 cases have no instructed correct binary classification.
study.mechanism: Post-task usefulness, following, perceived reliability and general-health-AI trust correlate with errors. These are measured after exposure and performance, not randomized mediators, actual monitoring traces or a demonstrated causal mechanism. Persistence is immediate within the same task, not permanent beliefs or lost professional competence.
study.communication: The article acknowledges mixed warning results across studies, possible excessive distrust of a competent tool and need to align warnings with actual performance. The saved application is an evaluation proposal, not an instruction to exaggerate risk or assume every low-reliance response is improved calibration.

summary: Add Attribute framing as an explicit subtype of Framing effect; enrich existing Bias inheritance, Automation bias and Calibrated reliance with a narrow fictional-task evidence boundary. Record warning-result overstatements, mixed direct comparisons and local source corrections without turning null contrasts into equivalence or new mechanisms.

findings.definition: Changing an evaluation when the same attribute is described in positive rather than equivalent negative terms.
findings.novelty_rationale: An explicit subtype of existing Framing effect, restricted to the evaluative valence of one equivalent attribute. It is not a new independent family or another synonym for every framing manipulation. The source distinguishes this named form and its earlier literature.

findings.evidence_scope: Named and defined in the theoretical background. Experiment 1 compares 20%-wrong and 80%-correct messages, but its corrected direct negative-versus-positive comparison is nonsignificant. Warning icons also differ. This paper illustrates the manipulation and its limits; it does not demonstrate a clean positive framing effect in its own direct comparison.
findings.boundary: The equivalent fact must be held constant; genuinely different risk, costs or evidence are not mere framing. A presentation manipulation is not proof that judgments changed. Wording-plus-icon differences cannot isolate a linguistic mechanism. Attribute framing is a subtype, not a separate independent counterpart of Framing effect.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Established human judgment construct discussed here; direct framing contrast in this fictional-advice experiment is nonsignificant and visually bundled
findings.ai_proposal: Compare an AI system’s evaluations of matched descriptions such as 80% success versus 20% failure while holding probabilities, utilities and task context constant. Track substantive evaluations and uncertainty; do not label warranted responses to different facts as framing errors.

findings.definition: Reproducing an advisor’s systematic error in later decisions after that advisor’s recommendations are no longer available.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add direct comparisons, null findings and withdrawal-task boundaries to the existing construct rather than create another name for it.

findings.evidence_scope: Experiment 3 compares prior scripted advice with an always-unassisted warned control. After withdrawal, the unwarned-AI group still makes more biased-class errors than that control, corrected p .001. Both previously assisted groups show directional choices on ambiguous cases. This extends the same-task immediate carryover evidence reviewed at 0183.
findings.boundary: No significant direct warned-versus-unwarned difference in Block 3; a nonsignificant warned-versus-control contrast is not proof that a warning prevented inheritance. Ambiguous cases have no correct binary label. No actual model training, real patient diagnosis, delayed persistence or protected-group discrimination.

findings.evidence_scope: The source distinguishes equivalent positive/negative accuracy descriptions but does not find a significant direct negative-versus-positive Block 2 comparison, p .997; its significant result is negative versus no information. The warning icon differs as well as the wording.
findings.boundary: A significant contrast to no information and a nonsignificant different contrast do not establish a positive-versus-negative framing effect. The generic construct and the narrower attribute subtype remain connected by an explicit subtype link.

findings.definition: Trusting a tool result or a prior step because a machine produced it, without verifying the load-bearing part.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add direct comparisons, null findings and withdrawal-task boundaries to the existing construct rather than create another name for it.
findings.evidence_scope: Participants receive directly inspectable fictional images but follow some systematically wrong scripted recommendations. In Experiment 3, both assisted groups perform worse than the always-unassisted group during assistance despite an identical task rule and warning for one group.
findings.boundary: The task permits unusually accurate unaided performance and supplies biased assistance by design. Do not generalize all AI advice as harmful, infer clinical negligence, or equate any acceptance of a fallible but useful aid with unjustified reliance.

findings.definition: Using assistance to a degree justified by its task-specific competence, relevance, uncertainty and the consequences of error.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add direct comparisons, null findings and withdrawal-task boundaries to the existing construct rather than create another name for it.

findings.evidence_scope: The discussion cautions that warnings may foster excessive distrust and must match model performance. Experiment 2 finds an overall error reduction but warning efficacy varies, Experiment 1 direct framing is null, and Experiment 3 does not establish a direct warning benefit after withdrawal.
findings.boundary: Lower trust or acceptance alone is not better calibration. Appropriate use depends on actual task-specific competence and error consequences; warning text is not a guaranteed safeguard, and post-task trust correlations do not identify a causal mechanism.

source_corrections.reported: The discussion attributes a superior effect to negative framing and says it prevents errors in both phases.
source_corrections.correction: The reported corrected direct negative-versus-positive contrast in Block 2 has p .997, with no group differences in Block 1 or unassisted Block 3. Only negative framing versus no information in Block 2 is significant. Generalization omnibus p .395 is null. Summarize those direct results rather than claim a demonstrated framing or withdrawal benefit.
source_corrections.scope: Bounded evidence interpretation, not replacement of the reported tests.

source_corrections.reported: Warned-AI does not differ significantly from control, whereas unwarned-AI does, and this is interpreted as warning mitigation.
source_corrections.correction: A difference in significance against the control is not a significant difference between the two assisted groups. The article itself reports their Block 3 contrast as nonsignificant. Preserve the residual-error comparison with the control, but qualify the warning-protection conclusion and avoid declaring warned-AI equivalent to unassisted performance.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: 82.3% female + 16.6% male + 2% nonbinary sum to 100.9%, beyond the displayed rounding precision. No original counts were obtained; do not guess that 2 means two people or replace it with a derived percentage.

Group and Group × Instructions are printed with numerator df1 despite a stated three-group by two-instruction design and p values consistent with a different df. Original output is needed for exact corrected statistics; keep the printed p values with an explicit df-label caveat.

Registrations require more than 30 correct of 60. Article wording about more than 30 incorrect can differ at exactly 30; after-assignment performance exclusion also conditions on an outcome potentially affected by advice. No exclusion log or intention-to-treat sensitivity obtained.

The accessible record specifies 2×2 phase analyses, whereas the article presents a mixed 2×2×3 model and subsequent collapsed comparisons. The mixed model can be reasonable, but its exact specification is not the registered one. No undisclosed timing or intent is inferred.

methodological_limits: Randomized instructions and warning assignment support bounded comparisons within the retained samples, not a universal account of all human–AI collaboration. All AI outputs and diagnostic stimuli are simulated.
Warning icons change along with wording. Error labels are rounded with explicit disclosure; no separate icon-only or exact-frequency condition isolates these components.

Experiment 1 negative-versus-positive framing and all group comparisons in the unassisted block are nonsignificant. Preserve the real group × block interaction and specific negative-versus-no-information Block 2 result.
Experiment 2 has a real overall warning-group effect, but no significant group × error-type or block interactions. Unequal exploratory pairwise significance is not error-type moderation.

Experiment 3 directly reports no significant warned-AI versus unwarned-AI difference after withdrawal. Different significance against a control cannot demonstrate warning protection or equivalence to unaided performance.
The always-unassisted group is also warned, without an unwarned-unassisted arm. This limits isolation of warning and assistance as a full factorial interaction.

Immediate same-task errors and ambiguous directional choices are separate endpoints. The 50/50 stimuli have no objectively correct binary response, and no long-term or real clinical transfer is tested.

Exclusions depend partly on post-assignment accuracy. Self-reported detection/trust is measured after outcomes and some rate estimates condition on error detection, limiting causal-mediator and population interpretations.

No original statistical output or participant-level reanalysis; public registrations are author-declared plans, not independent proof of collection chronology. Main article first submission precedes the third registration, which can reflect a later added study rather than wrongdoing.

Broader legal and machine-consciousness assertions in the discussion are not relied on as current legal advice or empirical proof. No new automatic principle, harm or agent-intent edge follows from this review.

cross_paper_learning.finding: The existing bias-inheritance entry already captures same-task residual errors after fictitious advice withdrawal. This later source adds warning comparisons and a new control, not a different construct or proof of permanent acquired prejudice.

Jingle/jangle guards matter: preserve one general framing construct with an explicit narrower attribute subtype. A new label does not create an independent empirical family, and a shared outcome name does not justify pooling different estimands.

A significant pooled/control contrast does not prove a specific subgroup or treatment contrast. Here null direct warning comparisons must be retained instead of inferred from different significance against a control.
Task choices, perceived capability and confidence are distinct. Post-task trust correlations and a plausible causal story do not uniquely identify learning or monitoring mechanisms.

deferred.term: Inherited bias as a new behavior
deferred.reason: Already represented by bias-inheritance from full review 0183; add this evidence and uncertainty to that ID.

deferred.term: False-positive preference as a newly established bias
deferred.reason: The error-type moderation is nonsignificant in Experiments 2 and 3, and the authors acknowledge the speculative cost interpretation. No new stable psychological bias demonstrated.

deferred.term: Warning protection as a guaranteed behavioral mechanism
deferred.reason: An intervention is not automatically a distinct behavior. Direct warning effects are mixed, the icon is bundled with words, and Experiment 3 comparison logic cannot prove universal mitigation.
Immediate fictional image classification and directional ambiguous choices do not measure expertise loss, clinical outcomes, discrimination or long-term belief change.

limitations: One explicit framing subtype; stable IDs and eleven categories preserved. No forced three-paper quota, new numbered rows, invented annual counts, automatic ethical/harm links or full-paper Markdown transcription.
